title: HMAC
body:
A **message authentication code** is a keyed tag: $t = \text{MAC}(k, m)$, sent alongside the
message, recomputed by the receiver, and rejected if it disagrees. It buys **integrity and
authenticity** at once, which a bare [[Cryptographic Hash Function]] cannot, because anybody can
recompute an unkeyed digest and an attacker who edits the message just edits the digest too. The
secret key is what they lack.

It is [[Symmetric Key Cryptography|symmetric]]: both sides hold the same $k$, so a MAC proves the
message came from *someone holding the key* and cannot prove which one. That is the difference from
a [[Digital Signature]], and it is why a MAC gives no non-repudiation.

**HMAC** is the standard construction:

$$\text{HMAC}(k, m) = H\big((k \oplus \text{opad}) \,\|\, H((k \oplus \text{ipad}) \,\|\, m)\big)$$

Two passes of the hash with two different key-derived pads. It exists because the obvious
construction is broken: **$H(k \| m)$ falls to the length-extension attack.** In a Merkle-Damgård
hash the digest is the internal state, so an attacker who sees $H(k \| m)$ can continue hashing and
produce a valid tag for $m \| \text{pad} \| m'$ without ever knowing $k$. The outer hash in HMAC
truncates that chain: the length-extended value is not the final output, so the attack yields
nothing.

$H(m \| k)$ is also wrong, in a different way: a collision in $H$ gives two messages with the same
tag under every key.

Three things to keep:

- **Compare tags in constant time.** A byte-by-byte comparison that returns early leaks the correct
  tag one byte at a time to a timing attack, and the attack is practical over a network.
- **Encrypt-then-MAC.** MAC the ciphertext, and check the MAC before decrypting anything. The other
  orders have both produced real attacks, and this is what makes padding oracles impossible: you
  never reach the padding check on forged data. See [[Modes of Operation]].
- Authenticated encryption modes such as **GCM** and **ChaCha20-Poly1305** do encryption and
  authentication in one pass and should be preferred over assembling it yourself.
